??? quote "Dialogue"

    - Hello, hello! Do I know you? I feel as if I ought to. Forgive me; I spend most of my days with people who have been dead for ninety years, and they are much easier to remember.
    - Ah, my door-knocker! Every 'nothing' you brought me is pinned up on that board, see, with a little cross. A history is half crosses. The other half is goats.
    - The goat won, *Player*. I have found the diary-writer who said it lost. He voted against the goat. History is written by sore losers too, it turns out. Wonderful. Wonderful!
    - The colour of the sky on the day they walked. I have it on the very first page of the book now. Nana came and read it and said I had spelled her mother's name wrong. I had not. She was pleased anyway.
    - Now, what was I... yes. What would you like to know?
        - *Choice:* What are you writing?
        - *Choice:* Who were the Walkers?
        - *Choice:* What happened in the first winter?
        - *Choice:* What is this about Dog-Ear's script?
        - *Choice:* Nothing, thanks.
    - Urbanograd's first hundred years, told through the Walkers' own words: their letters, diaries and songs, and their children's. Eighteen years in this corner. Before that I taught children to read in my front room. Half the Table learned their letters there.
    - I would like to finish it before my eyes give out. I am not certain I will. So I write faster, and then I find a new letter, and I write slower again, because it deserves to be read properly.
    - About three hundred people who walked out of Selsior behind Juna Marrow, after the theatre guild had her cart hauled away. Painters too vulgar for the galleries, musicians too loud, tinkerers nobody would license. And more joined on the road, from Kaldemor, the harbours, the highlands.
    - My grandfather was one: a fiddler, whose songs Selsior's theatres would not hear. He sang them to me at bedtime, very badly. That is where all this began. I wanted to know who wrote them, and who sang them on the road.
    - Nobody knows. That is the honest answer, and I hate it. The Walkers wrote about the road, and about the spring after. Of the first winter itself: nothing. Not a letter. The Table's own record books begin after it.
    - Perhaps they were too cold and hungry to write. Perhaps the pages were burned for warmth. Perhaps somebody hid them. I would pay well for one page of it from an old attic. If you ever find one, run here. Walk. Do not fall.
    - Dog-Ear Tuck, at the Night Market, claims to own a script of Juna's play in her own hand. Ten years I have asked to see it. Ten years he has quoted me a line or two, grinned, and changed the subject to the weather.
    - Half of me believes it is real. The other half thinks it is the best joke in the city. Both halves keep going back to his stall. He knows it, the old rascal.
    - Goodbye, goodbye. If you see a pair of spectacles anywhere in the city, they are probably mine.
